title: Agile & Hybrid Ways of Working
sequence: Introduction. A consolidated view of agile and hybrid practice; each later topic adds its agile angle.

header.html: Cross-cutting: about 60% of exam items involve adaptive/agile or hybrid approaches, spread across People, Process and Business Environment. Touches nearly every task (stakeholders, team leadership, schedule "story points", scope/backlog, impediments, risk, change, value-based delivery).

Standard §4.2.2–4.2.3 (adaptive and hybrid approaches), Guide Section 5 tools (agile release planning, backlog management and refinement, burndown/burnup charts, daily coordination meeting, retrospectives, sprint review, velocity, visual controls, information radiators, customer talks and tests, design thinking), Section 4 artifacts (backlog, user stories, team charter), Glossary (definition of done, epic, iteration, MVP, sprint, story point, timebox)
Introduction. A consolidated view of agile and hybrid practice; each later topic adds its agile angle.

[Beyond PMBOK 8] = exam-relevant, but PMBOK 8 does not spell it out (Agile Practice Guide/Scrum Guide-style content, common exam practice, mock-exam style). PMBOK 8 mentions Scrum and other methods but does not define them in detail.

html:
1Agile Mindset and Values

  • Agile (glossary): a mindset of values and principles set out in the Manifesto for Agile Software Development. It is broader than any framework or method; agile approaches are adaptive approaches.
  • [Beyond PMBOK 8] The four Manifesto values: individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan. (The items on the right still have value; the left is valued more.)
  • [Beyond PMBOK 8] Principles in brief: satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery; welcome change; deliver frequently; business people and the team work together daily; build around motivated people and trust them; face-to-face conversation; working product is the primary measure of progress; sustainable pace; technical excellence; simplicity (maximize work not done); self-organizing teams; regular reflection and adjustment.
  • Servant leadership (PMBOK 8): leading by focusing on understanding and addressing the needs and development of team members to enable the highest team performance, in service to the project's business objectives (Topic 25).
  • Adaptive approaches in the Standard: a clear vision at the start; requirements progressively elaborated by feedback; iterations of 1 to 4 weeks with demonstrations; whole-team planning; often 3 to 9 team members; some methods favor colocation.

2Roles in Adaptive Projects

PMBOK 8: the function matters, not the title. In adaptive and agile environments product owner or product manager may carry some project management tasks; titles such as scrum master, agile coach, agile manager, team lead, development team can share them. Coordination can be centralized (top-down, one accountable person such as a PM) or distributed (decision-making and authority spread across empowered individuals; the team may self-organize and a facilitator role can rotate).

Role Responsibilities
Product owner (glossary) Responsible for maximizing the value of the product and accountable for the end product; usually prepares and owns the product backlog, ranked by business value; the voice of the customer; accepts work
Scrum master / agile coach / project manager as servant leader Facilitates, removes impediments, coaches the team and organization, shields the team from outside disruption, protects the process; does not assign tasks or micromanage
Project (development) team Cross-functional, self-organizing, ideally dedicated; decides how to build; sizes backlog items and commits to the iteration scope
Sponsor, customers, end users Provide direction, resources and feedback; engage mainly through the product owner and reviews

[Beyond PMBOK 8] Scrum framework summary:

Element Detail
Roles Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers (one small Scrum team; the Scrum Guide says 10 or fewer)
Events Sprint (timebox up to one month) containing: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum (15 minutes), Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective
Artifacts and commitments Product Backlog (product goal), Sprint Backlog (sprint goal), Increment (definition of done)
Values Commitment, focus, openness, respect, courage

PMBOK 8 equivalents: iteration (sprint), iteration planning, daily coordination meeting, iteration/sprint review, retrospective.

3Planning Layers and Backlogs

  • Product vision → product roadmap → release plan → iteration plan → daily plan. Agile release planning gives a high-level timeline (typically 3 to 6 months) built from the roadmap and vision; it fixes the number of iterations in the release and shows which features arrive when.
  • Backlog (PMBOK 8 artifact): an ordered list of work, often user stories, prioritized by the business; it reflects current needs and a reprioritized plan for the remaining work.
Backlog Contents
Product backlog Complete list of desired requirements, features, epics and user stories; the overall scope and vision; usually prepared by the product owner
Release backlog Subset planned for a specific release (may span several iterations)
Iteration (sprint) backlog Selected stories plus tasks to complete the committed work in the current iteration
  • Backlog management is how adaptive teams manage change: items are ranked by business value or importance to the customer, sized by the team, with dependencies and constraints considered, so the highest-value items are delivered next.
  • Backlog refinement: progressive elaboration and reprioritization to prepare the work for upcoming iterations (constantly review, revise, rank, edit).
  • Epic: large body of related work that organizes requirements hierarchically; split into user stories.
  • User story: a brief description of an outcome from a stakeholder's perspective, "a promise for a conversation"; typically states the role (who benefits), the goal (what they need) and the motivation (the benefit). Acceptance criteria focus on the specific functionality and end-user expectations to be fulfilled.
  • MVP (minimum viable product): the fewest features that deliver value, defining the first release.
  • Definition of done (DoD): checklist of all criteria that must be met for a deliverable to be ready for customer use (quality, tests, compliance). Definition of ready (also "full kit"): checklist confirming work is ready to start, which minimizes rework.
  • Prioritization methods (PMBOK 8): MoSCoW (must, should, could, will not have), 100-point method, cost of delay, Kano analysis.
  • [Beyond PMBOK 8] WSJF (weighted shortest job first): priority = cost of delay ÷ job size, where cost of delay = user or business value + time criticality + risk reduction or opportunity enablement. The highest score goes first, so small, urgent, valuable items rise.
  • [Beyond PMBOK 8] Spike: a short timeboxed investigation to reduce a technical or design unknown before committing to a story.
  • [Beyond PMBOK 8] Story map: a two-dimensional backlog. The backbone of user activities runs left to right, the details sit below each activity, and horizontal slices form releases. The first release (the MVP) must work end to end, a "walking skeleton": scan the backbone column by column, and a column with nothing in release 1 means a customer cannot finish the journey.

4The Iteration Cycle

Event (PMBOK 8 / Scrum name) Purpose and key points
Iteration planning (sprint planning) Clarify backlog items, acceptance criteria and effort; the team determines what it can accomplish and commits to the scope; scope is chosen from the prioritized backlog [Beyond: sprint goal; planning timebox up to 8 hours for a one-month sprint]
Daily coordination meeting (daily scrum, stand-up) No more than 15 minutes; what was done yesterday, plan for today, obstacles; enables self-direction and visibility, accountability and quick problem-solving
Iteration / sprint review (demo) At the end of the iteration the team demonstrates completed work to stakeholders and solicits feedback; feedback shapes the backlog. Needs real discussion time, not a one-way demo, and the real customers or end users in the room, not internal staff only: high feature completion with falling user ratings is output without outcome (Topic 10) [Beyond: review up to 4 hours for a one-month sprint]
Retrospective Regular workshop (at minimum at the end of each iteration) where the whole team explores what worked and what did not to improve process and product; outcomes are actionable with owners. Any lessons-learned session in any approach can be called a retrospective [Beyond: up to 3 hours for a one-month sprint]
Backlog refinement Ongoing preparation of upcoming work
In-progress postmortems Periodic structured reviews of current performance during the life cycle (not only at the end)

Rules of thumb [Beyond PMBOK 8 — exam practice]: the team's commitment inside an iteration is protected; new requests go to the product owner and the backlog for a later iteration (an iteration can be canceled only by the product owner in Scrum); changes of direction reflect feedback at reviews.

5Estimating and Measuring Progress

  • Story points (glossary): a unit estimating the relative level of effort to implement a user story. Teams compare items better than they predict durations, so relative sizing is simpler without losing accuracy. Common techniques named in PMBOK 8: planning poker, story points, T-shirt sizing, plus Delphi, analogous, parametric, bottom-up and PERT estimating (Topic 16). Tasks may still be estimated in hours.
  • Velocity (PMBOK 8): the rate at which deliverables are produced, validated and accepted within a predefined interval; used to forecast how much a team can take on. Beyond PMBOK 8 It is team-specific; do not use it to compare teams or push inflation, and it measures output, not value; also track outcomes and customer usage.

Chart Shows Notes
Burndown chart Work remaining vs time left in a timebox Can show story points remaining or risk exposure reduced
Iteration burndown Remaining iteration work vs an ideal line; a trend line forecasts completion Reveals variance within the iteration
Burnup chart Work completed toward a milestone, with total scope as a line across the top [Beyond PMBOK 8] Scope changes are visible: the scope line moves when scope is added or removed
Cumulative flow diagram (glossary) Features completed over time, in other states and in the backlog [Beyond PMBOK 8] A band that keeps widening marks a state where items arrive faster than they leave: the bottleneck. A flat Done line means little is finishing

  • Kanban cycle time = from a task starting until it is completed. Lead time = from a task being put on the board until it is delivered to the customer (can be unpredictable if the Ready column is reordered).
  • [Beyond PMBOK 8] Flow measures: throughput (items finished per period), WIP (items in progress), cycle time (start to finish), lead time (request to delivery), velocity (story points per iteration) and takt time (available time ÷ demand: the pace needed to meet demand). By Little's law, average cycle time = WIP ÷ throughput, so a lower WIP shortens cycle time.

6Flow, Kanban, Lean and Continuous Improvement

  • Flow-based scheduling optimizes the flow of work through the system: maximize throughput, minimize waste. Kanban is a visual workflow method that limits work in process (WIP) (lean principles; continuous delivery without overburdening the team). When a column nears its WIP limit, the team swarms to help work that is slowing the flow.
  • Visual controls / information radiators: highly visible displays of progress (task boards, Kanban boards, burn charts, impediment lists) updated frequently; "low tech, high touch" is fine. Information radiators sit where people actually look, not buried in a tool.
  • Theory of constraints (TOC): find and address the biggest limiting factor; applied to projects as critical chain project management (Topic 16).
  • Lean: eliminate waste; value stream mapping documents the steps and time in a process to find waste, from customer request to value realized.
  • Continuous improvement: ongoing incremental improvement using PDCA, Lean, TQM, Six Sigma, five focusing steps (Topic 31).
  • [Beyond PMBOK 8] Kanban principles: visualize work; limit WIP; manage flow; make policies explicit; implement feedback loops; improve collaboratively. Kanban has no mandatory roles or iterations.

7Team Environment and Collaboration

  • Team charter (Section 4 artifact): values, agreements and operating guidelines (communication, decision-making, conflict resolution, meeting guidelines, team agreements). Works best when the team develops it; review and update periodically and revisit it with new members.
  • Colocation (physical closeness) improves communication and productivity and can be temporary; virtual collaboration tools support distributed teams.
  • Dedicated, cross-functional members reduce context switching and waiting; part-time sharing is a risk.
  • Customer talks and tests: direct customer interaction and feedback during development and testing build trust and quality.
  • Design thinking: nonlinear, iterative, human-centered process (understand users, challenge assumptions, redefine problems, prototype and test), popular in new product development.

8Agile Across the Performance Domains

Domain Agile / adaptive approach (PMBOK 8)
Governance Lightweight governance; periodic reviews; right-sized controls; leadership from the whole team
Scope The backlog reflects current needs; scope delivered adaptively; completion measured against product requirements
Schedule Release and iteration planning, flow-based scheduling; timeboxes; progress via burn charts
Finance Budget can be allocated quarterly and revised quarterly; track spend per iteration against delivered value [Beyond: sprint-level burn vs value]
Stakeholders Continuous feedback, daily coordination meetings, collaboration platforms, reviews with real feedback time, information radiators
Resources Self-organizing, dedicated teams; distributed management and leadership; servant leaders
Risk Risk assessment at the start of each iteration, risk review at the end, risk-adjusted backlog; risks visible in the backlog
Quality DoD with testing and compliance inside every iteration (shift-left), acceptance criteria per story

9Hybrid Ways of Working

PMBOK 8: most real projects benefit from a hybrid mix; patterns and DA levels are in Topic 03. Practical guidance:

Topic Hybrid practice
Choosing Per deliverable or stream: stable, regulated, long-lead items predictive; uncertain items adaptive
Planning Baseline fixed elements; roadmap and backlog for the rest; milestones plus iteration plans
Reporting [Beyond PMBOK 8] A schedule that executives recognize (milestones, fixed dates) with iteration detail beneath; avoid converting a backlog into a false-precision Gantt chart
Metrics Earned value or milestone metrics for predictive streams; burn charts, velocity, cycle time for agile ones; one consolidated view for governance
Change control Tailored: routine backlog changes flow through the product owner; changes above a contractual or baseline threshold use formal change control
Procurement / contracts Agreements that allow iterative scope (e.g., time-and-materials or target-cost elements) with controls; check Topic 22
Compliance and documentation Build regulatory evidence into the DoD and iteration deliverables rather than a big final audit
Team boundaries Make clear who decides what; align governance reviews to iteration cadence

10Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid (Ways of Working)

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Who manages Project manager (centralized) Self-organizing team with product owner and scrum master (distributed) Shared; PM plus product owner
Plans Detailed baselined plan Vision, roadmap, release and iteration plans, frequent replanning Baselines plus backlog
Change Formal change control Backlog reprioritization Tailored mix
Progress measure Earned value, milestones, schedule variance Working increments, velocity, burn charts, cumulative flow Both
Quality Plans, inspections, audits DoD, continuous testing, reviews, retrospectives Both
Customer role Specifies up front; accepts at milestones Collaborates continuously Both
Risk handling Register, reviews at gates, reserves Risk-adjusted backlog, per-iteration review Both

11Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Be a servant leader. Facilitate, remove impediments, coach, shield the team. Do not assign tasks, dictate how to build, or enforce rules individually. When team members breach their own charter, facilitate a team discussion on honoring it.
  2. The team self-organizes and commits to the iteration scope. The PM does not add work mid-iteration to please a senior stakeholder; route new requests to the product owner and backlog and represent the team's capacity.
  3. The product owner owns priorities and value. Conflicting requests are made visible and discussed; the product owner orders by value; stakeholders do not go around the product owner to the team.
  4. Impediments get removed, not just logged. Prioritize by impact; the PM works with outside groups to clear recurring blockers rather than adding them to a list every day.
  5. Retrospectives must change something. Pick a few improvements and put them in the next backlog; inspect the improvement process itself when nothing changes.
  6. Reviews need feedback, and real customers. Build discussion time into reviews and include end customers, not only internal proxies. Do not wait weeks for feedback by email.
  7. Quality is built in through the definition of done (automated tests, accessibility, compliance) rather than a late testing phase.
  8. Velocity is output, not value. Shift measures toward customer usage and outcomes; do not raise velocity targets to "get more".
  9. Pick the right chart. Burnup shows scope growth; burndown shows remaining work. If scope grows, explain it rather than pressuring the team.
  10. WIP limits and flow. At a limit, stop starting and help finish (swarm). Do not add work to a bottlenecked column.
  11. Transparency. Make progress and risks visible where stakeholders look (information radiators, backlog).
  12. Agile does not mean no planning or no governance. Plan at multiple levels, report in terms stakeholders recognize, and tailor controls to contractual or regulatory needs (hybrid).
  13. Revisit team agreements when membership changes, with the whole team including the newcomer.
  14. When funding or the need ends, close properly: agree closure criteria and move remaining backlog value to the product owner.

12Exam Q&A

12.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A burnup chart shows 60 story points completed, and the scope line has risen from 120 to 150 points since kickoff. At its current pace of 10 points per iteration, how many more iterations does the team need?

  • ATwelve, because the 30 added points count on top of the 90 remaining
  • BNine, because 90 points remain against the current scope line
  • CSix, because the original scope leaves only 60 points to complete
  • DFifteen, because the whole current scope still has to be delivered
Show the answer

Answer: B. Remaining work is the scope line minus the completed line: 150 minus 60 leaves 90 points, which is nine iterations at 10 points each. Six ignores the added scope, twelve counts the added points twice, and fifteen ignores the work already completed.

S2A customer asks how long it takes from the moment a request is added to the team's board until it reaches the customer. Which Kanban measure answers that question?

  • AVelocity, measured as the amount of work accepted in each iteration
  • BCycle time, measured from starting the work until the item is complete
  • CLead time, measured from entering the board until delivery to the customer
  • DBurndown, measured as the work remaining against the time left
Show the answer

Answer: C. Lead time runs from the moment an item is put on the board until it is delivered to the customer, while cycle time starts only when work begins. Velocity and burndown describe team output and remaining work, not the elapsed time of a single request.

S3Developers often start stories whose acceptance criteria are unclear, then stop to ask questions and redo work. Which agile practice would reduce this rework?

  • AA second daily meeting dedicated to clarifying all of the open questions
  • BA definition of ready that confirms stories are clear and sized before an iteration
  • CA longer definition of done with extra test steps at the end of each story
  • DA signed requirements specification for the whole product before development begins
Show the answer

Answer: B. A definition of ready, also called full kit, is a checklist confirming that work is ready to start, which minimizes rework. The definition of done governs completion, a complete up-front specification is a predictive habit, and extra meetings treat the symptom.

S4In retrospectives, colleagues keep blaming the tester for defects that reach customers, and the tester has stopped speaking. What should the project manager do?

  • AReset ground rules so the team examines process causes and everyone can speak safely
  • BAsk the tester to prepare a defect report for the whole team to review
  • CRemove the tester from the retrospectives so that the discussion stays calm and productive
  • DMove the blame discussion into a private meeting with the tester and manager
Show the answer

Answer: A. Retrospectives explore what worked and what did not in process and product, and they need an environment in which people feel safe to speak. Excluding the tester, demanding a defect report or moving the discussion into private keeps the focus on one person.

S5A support team handling a continuous stream of incoming tickets asks whether it must adopt two-week sprints to be agile. Which advice is best?

  • AUse a flow-based method such as Kanban with WIP limits, which suits continuous work
  • BHandle each ticket in arrival order without limiting how many are open
  • CAdopt two-week sprints, because iterations are required for any work to count as agile
  • DPlan the full year of tickets in advance and track them with a Gantt chart
Show the answer

Answer: A. Flow-based scheduling with a visual board and limited work in process suits a continuous stream of work, and Kanban has no mandatory iterations or roles. Forced sprints, a year-long plan or unlimited parallel work do not fit the nature of the work.

S6On a Kanban board the System Test column is at its WIP limit while finished development items queue up. What should the team do?

  • ARaise the WIP limit so that the queue can keep moving forward
  • BSkip testing for the urgent items until the queue has cleared
  • CStart new development items so that the developers stay busy
  • DSwarm to help finish testing before pulling in any new work
Show the answer

Answer: D. WIP limits expose bottlenecks, so the team finishes work already in progress by swarming on the constraint before starting more. Starting items, raising the limit or skipping tests ignores the signal or lowers quality.

S7The team's daily coordination meeting has grown to 40 minutes of status debate, and several members now skip it. What should the project manager do?

  • AReplace it with written status updates that the project manager collects
  • BChange it to a weekly meeting so that attendance improves again
  • CLet it run as long as needed so that each topic is fully resolved
  • DRefocus it on yesterday's work, today's plan and obstacles, within 15 minutes
Show the answer

Answer: D. The daily coordination meeting is a short event of no more than 15 minutes covering what was done, what is planned and what blocks the work, which keeps visibility and quick problem-solving. Written updates, longer sessions or a weekly rhythm remove the daily coordination it exists to provide.

S8The backlog contains a story titled 'Improve the checkout', and the developers say they can neither estimate nor test it. What should the project manager help the team do?

  • AMove it to the end of the backlog until the sponsor writes a detailed specification for it
  • BRefine it with the product owner into stories with clear goals and acceptance criteria
  • CEstimate it at the largest size and start with the easiest parts first
  • DAsk the developers to define the details on their own while building it
Show the answer

Answer: B. A user story states who benefits, what they need and why, with acceptance criteria, and backlog refinement turns vague items into estimable, testable stories. Guessing the size, letting developers invent the detail or waiting for a specification skips that conversation.

S9Two team members disagree about a technical approach and ask the project manager to decide. What should the project manager do?

  • ADecide immediately so that the team can keep moving without delay
  • BEscalate the disagreement to the sponsor for a final ruling today
  • CFacilitate a discussion so the team decides, and coach them on resolving it
  • DLet the more senior of the two members make the final decision
Show the answer

Answer: C. Self-organizing teams make their own technical decisions, with the project manager facilitating and coaching. Deciding for them, escalating or defaulting to seniority removes the team's ownership.

S10Stories wait days for clarification each iteration because the business owner who knows the answers is rarely available. How should the project manager respond?

  • AReplace the owner with whichever business user is free first
  • BLog the delays and discuss them again at the next retrospective
  • CLet the team assume the likely answers and correct any mistakes at the iteration review
  • DWork with the sponsor to secure the owner's availability or delegated decision rights
Show the answer

Answer: D. An unavailable decision-maker is an impediment outside the team's control, so the project manager works with those who have authority to remove it, for example through scheduled availability or decision rights given to the product owner. Guessing, logging or swapping the owner at random leaves the cause.

S11A single agile team of 15 members spends most of its daily meeting and planning sessions on coordination, and decisions are slow. What would be a sensible adjustment?

  • ASplit into two smaller cross-functional teams that coordinate through shared goals
  • BAdd a coordination layer where one lead relays decisions between members
  • CKeep the size and extend the planning sessions so everyone can contribute
  • DCut the team to its most senior members and reassign everyone else
Show the answer

Answer: A. Adaptive teams tend to work best with about three to nine members, so a larger group is split into cross-functional teams that coordinate. A relay layer, longer sessions or discarding most of the team do not restore fast, shared decision-making.

S12A newly promoted sales director messages individual developers to switch tasks several times a week, and the team's delivery is becoming erratic. What should the project manager do?

  • AAsk the developers to follow the director's instructions for the moment, to keep the peace in the team
  • BTell the developers to ignore all messages that come from the director
  • CMeet the director to explain how requests enter the backlog through the product owner
  • DReport the director's behavior to the sponsor as a breach of the process
Show the answer

Answer: C. The product owner owns priorities and value, so stakeholders route requests through the backlog rather than directing the team. The project manager engages the director to explain the channel and its effect on delivery instead of ignoring, obeying or reporting.

12.2 Recall Q&As

R1What is the PMBOK 8 definition of agile?

Show the answer

A mindset of values and principles set out in the Manifesto for Agile Software Development.

R2[Beyond PMBOK 8] State the four Agile Manifesto values.

Show the answer

Individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan.

R3What are the three backlog types?

Show the answer

Product backlog, release backlog, iteration (sprint) backlog.

R4What does a user story contain?

Show the answer

A brief description from a stakeholder's perspective: role, goal and motivation, with acceptance criteria.

R5What is the definition of done?

Show the answer

A checklist of all criteria a deliverable must meet to be ready for customer use.

R6How long is a daily coordination meeting?

Show the answer

No more than 15 minutes: yesterday, today, obstacles.

R7How often are retrospectives held?

Show the answer

Frequently, at minimum at the end of each iteration; the outputs are actions with owners.

R8What is velocity?

Show the answer

The rate at which deliverables are produced, validated and accepted within a predefined interval.

R9Burndown vs burnup?

Show the answer

Burndown shows work remaining against time; burnup shows work completed against total scope, making scope changes visible.

R10What is a story point?

Show the answer

A relative estimate of the effort to implement a user story.

R11Cycle time vs lead time?

Show the answer

Cycle time runs from work start to completion; lead time runs from entering the board to delivery to the customer.

R12What do WIP limits do?

Show the answer

Cap work in process to expose bottlenecks and keep flow smooth; teams swarm to finish work nearing the limit.

R13[Beyond PMBOK 8] Name the Scrum events.

Show the answer

Sprint, sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review, sprint retrospective.

R14What is MVP?

Show the answer

The minimum viable product: the fewest features that deliver value, used to define the first release.

13Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Agile Mindset of values and principles (Manifesto); adaptive approach
Servant leader Facilitate, coach, remove impediments, shield the team; don't command
Product owner Maximizes value; owns and orders the backlog
Team Self-organizing, cross-functional, ideally dedicated; commits to iteration scope
Planning layers Vision → roadmap → release (3 to 6 months) → iteration (1 to 4 weeks) → daily
Backlogs Product, release, iteration; ranked by value; refined continuously
User story Role, goal, motivation + acceptance criteria; epics split into stories
DoD / DoR Ready for customer use / ready to start
Events Iteration planning, daily coordination (≤15 min), review (demo + feedback), retrospective (actions)
Estimates Story points, planning poker, T-shirt sizing; velocity = accepted work per interval
Charts Burndown (remaining), burnup (completed vs scope), cumulative flow
Flow Kanban, WIP limits, swarming; cycle time vs lead time; TOC; Lean; value stream mapping
Transparency Information radiators / visual controls where stakeholders look
Risk and money Risk-adjusted backlog; per-iteration risk review; quarterly budgets revised quarterly
Hybrid Tailor per deliverable; milestones + iterations; tailored change control; unified reporting
First-action pattern Facilitate and remove blockers, protect the iteration, make things visible, route change through the backlog
